Trip info

✨ Highlights▾
  • Roquebrune Rock: 373 m and three monumental crosses by Bernar Venet
  • La Gaillarde Gallo-Roman fish pond: three basins listed as a historic monument since 1939
  • Sainte-Roseline Chapel: mummy in a crystal reliquary and a mosaic by Marc Chagall
  • Blavet Gorges: red rhyolite canyon and Mueron Cave, occupied in 10,000 BC
  • Fréjus: 1st-century amphitheater and 5th-century baptistery, among France's oldest
☀️ Weather▾

Best time to visit: May–June and September–October, around 18 to 26°C, with the sea still warm in September. Avoid July–August: oppressive heat, an overcrowded coast and restricted access to forested hills due to fire risk. Winters are mild but rainy, with spells of dry, cold mistral winds.

📋 Notes▾

The 33 stops are logical waypoints, not overnight stays: the itinerary assumes Roquebrune-sur-Argens serves as the main base for trips out to the Gulf of Saint-Tropez, the Maures, the Estérel and the upper Var. Allow 10 full days, with several stops combined on the same day.

Roquebrune-sur-Argens: sea, villages and the Var in 10 days : 33 stops

Roquebrune Sur Argens

🛏️ Suggested base : Roquebrune Sur Argens
★★★★☆
1

Start with the Castrum: it's the part of Roquebrune-sur-Argens that has changed least since the year 1000. The fortified walls date from around the 10th century, and rue des Portiques below is lined with 16th-century arcaded houses beneath the belfry. Walk through in late afternoon, when the arcades cast patterns of shadow and the groups have left.

⏱ 60 min
2

Built on remains from the 11th and 12th centuries, the Saint-Pierre-Saint-Paul parish church hides a far more spectacular interior than expected behind its restrained Gothic façade. It's listed on the historic monuments inventory. Step inside as you leave the Castrum—it's two minutes away: the contrast between outside and inside is what gives the visit its charm.

⏱ 30 min
3

A free museum with an ice house beneath your feet: the Maison du Patrimoine occupies a former stable built in 1883 on impasse Barbacane, and its glass floor protects a 17th-century ice house discovered in 2002. The rest tells the story of the town from prehistory to the cork industry. Free entry, but closed on weekends outside the tourist season: check before heading up to the village.

⏱ 45 min

Diving in the Calanque Saint-Barthélemy

Activities

The smell of cocoa gives away the Maison du Chocolat et Cacao before you even see it: it occupies a former chapel in the old center of Roquebrune-sur-Argens and opened in June 2015. Inside, you follow the village's chocolate history and its famous Rocher, a lavender-honey nougat coated in chocolate.

⏱ 45 min

If you have an extra hour, follow the 7 Fontaines route through the lanes and small squares of Roquebrune-sur-Argens. You'll pass the 18th-century Fontaine Vieille and the clock tower rising above the 16th-century ramparts. The map is free at the tourist office, and the route stays in the shade: perfect between 2pm and 4pm in summer.

⏱ 60 min

Rocher De Roquebrune

🛏️ Suggested base : Roquebrune Sur Argens · 3 km
★★★★☆
1

Roquebrune Rock rises to 373 meters and can be spotted from the A8 highway: a red mass set between the Maures and the Estérel, without truly belonging to either. At the summit, the monumental Trois Croix are the work of Bernar Venet, and the panorama stretches through 360°, from the sea to the Maures. Expect to use your hands as much as your feet: the last few meters require climbing with the help of cables.

⏱ 120 min
2

Built in the 16th century, the Notre-Dame de la Roquette chapel belonged to a former Trinitarian convent, some ruins of which remain nearby. A forest fire severely damaged it in 1962, and tile thefts did the rest in the 1980s–1990s. The site is listed and the building is fragile: look, don't climb on it.

⏱ 30 min
3

Locals call it the Saint Trou: a very narrow cleft in Roquebrune Rock with a legend attached. A young woman being pursued supposedly implored the Virgin, and the rock opened to let her pass; they say only virtuous souls can cross it. Trail markers peter out in this area and cairns take over: don't set out without a map.

⏱ 45 min

Activities

Park at the Pont d'Argens parking lot, facing the Saint-Roch chapel, to tackle the climb to the Trois Croix on Roquebrune Rock via the marked trail. Views of the Argens plain and the Estérel open up at the large rock slab halfway along. Access to the hills is restricted in summer according to fire risk: the prefecture publishes a map daily.

⏱ 240 min

The Hautes Roques alternative route is not a family walk: sections equipped with cables, rock steps and a summit perched above the cliffs of Roquebrune Rock. It starts at the Hautes Roques parking lot, north of the hills. Hiking boots are essential, and turn back immediately if the rock is wet.

⏱ 300 min

Lac De L Arena

🛏️ Suggested base : Roquebrune Sur Argens · 1 km
★★★★☆
1

A former sand quarry turned lake: Lake Aréna, also called Lake Perrin, covers some thirty hectares of fresh water at the foot of Roquebrune Rock. The site has Natura 2000 status and wildlife has reclaimed it. The best photo angle is from the south shore, early in the morning, when the rock glows red above the still water.

⏱ 45 min
2

Aréna Beach borders Lake Perrin on the water sports center side: sand, deck chairs and a head-on view of Roquebrune Rock. It's a lake beach, not a sea beach: fresh water, no waves, no salt. A flat, easy trail circles the lake, ideal for letting your meal settle before heading out.

⏱ 45 min

Activities

Rent a paddleboard at the Arena Plage water sports center on Lake Aréna, and head as far as the passage toward the Argens: the corridor of vegetation linking the lake to the river takes a little paddling effort to reach. The lake waters stay calm, and children can stand on their boards without any drama. The center is open from May 1 to September 30, not before.

⏱ 90 min

The inflatable water park at Aréna Plage is mainly worthwhile for kids: slides, obstacle courses and a separate Aquakids area for little ones, all set up on Lake Aréna. The multi-activity packages advertised by the regional tourist office cost around €35 per adult and €30 per child. In July–August, arrive when it opens at 9:30am.

⏱ 180 min

If you're passing through on a Sunday morning, the weekly flea market is held right next to Lake Aréna, summer and winter. It's more a local gathering than a tourist market. Follow up with the fruit and vegetable market at the water sports center to put together a picnic and eat it by the water.

⏱ 60 min

Dolmens De L Agriotier

🛏️ Suggested base : Sainte Maxime · 9 km
★★★★☆
1

Listed as early as 1910, the Agriotier dolmens stand at an altitude of 198 meters in the hills above Les Issambres. They remind us that the valley was inhabited well before the Romans and their fish ponds. You reach them along trails climbing from the coast. Bring water: shade is scarce and access to the hills is restricted from June 21 to September 20.

⏱ 45 min

Activities

Climb to the Agriotier dolmens from the coast at Les Issambres: the slope is steep and the trail passes through cork oaks and mimosas. The view looks down over Saint-Aygulf and the Estérel. Bring water: there's nowhere to get supplies along the way, and the sun beats down hard in summer.

⏱ 90 min

Vivier Gallo Romain De La Gaillarde

🛏️ Suggested base : Sainte Maxime · 8 km
★★★★☆
1

Three basins carved into the rock, steps from the departmental road: the Gallo-Roman fish pond of La Gaillarde has been listed as a historic monument since 1939. Fish were kept alive there, and garum was probably made there too, a sauce of fermented fish guts whose smell kept villas at a distance. The low walls are visible a few centimeters below the water: come when the sea is calm, or you'll see nothing.

⏱ 30 min
2

Aligned north–south in a 20-meter-long cove, the fish pond at Pointe de la Calle used the prevailing winds and swell to refresh its water. It belonged to a villa in the La Gaillarde valley, a kilometer away. There's an explanatory plaque on site and nothing else: don't expect a site with visitor facilities.

⏱ 20 min

Activities

Walk from Port Ferréol: the stretch of coastal path leading to the Gallo-Roman fish pond of La Gaillarde takes just a few minutes and connects to the corniche des Cigales. There are few suitable places to swim here, and it's almost deserted, even in August. That's precisely what makes it pleasant.

⏱ 45 min

Les Issambres

🛏️ Suggested base : Sainte Maxime · 6 km
★★★★☆
1

Les Issambres has 8 km of coves and beaches between the Gulf of Saint-Tropez and Fréjus: it's Roquebrune-sur-Argens' window onto the sea. Its heart beats on place San-Peïre, around the port and café terraces. San-Peïre beach and its port have Blue Flag status. Parking is difficult in August: come before 10am or leave the car and take the bus.

⏱ 60 min
2

In winter, you smell the mimosa in the La Gaillarde valley before you even see it: the flowering trees turn the trail into a yellow avenue above Les Issambres. Below, La Gaillarde beach also has Blue Flag status. There are three routes to choose from depending on your fitness. February is mimosa month, not July.

⏱ 60 min

Activities

Take the coastal path at Les Issambres: 8 km one way with no elevation gain, following the old customs officers' path from the First Empire. It runs between coves, rocks and umbrella pines, with the Gulf of Saint-Tropez and the Estérel as a backdrop. Check bus schedules for the return, or you'll walk 16 km instead of 8.

⏱ 150 min

The municipal sailing center at Les Issambres remains the simplest way to get out to sea without breaking the bank: courses and rentals, with options for all levels. You can also go diving, water skiing and jet skiing in the bay. Book the day before in summer; morning slots go first.

⏱ 120 min

Sainte Maxime

🛏️ Suggested base : Sainte Maxime
★★★☆☆
1

Construction of Sainte-Maxime's Tour Carrée began in 1520 under the abbey of Le Thoronet. Until 1935, it served as a lord's residence, a gun tower, a granary, a prison, a school and a town hall. The dungeon remains accessible within the walls. Listed in 1977, it now houses the Maison des Traditions. The town offers guided tours: ask in advance.

⏱ 45 min
2

The Maximois nickname the Pointe des Sardinaux little Corsica: rocks, pines and clear water, a few minutes from the center of Sainte-Maxime. It is the least built-up spot along the town's 11 km of coastline. Wear closed-toe shoes: it is more slippery than it looks.

⏱ 60 min

Activities

Walk through Sainte-Maxime's covered market in the morning: Provence AOC olive oil, Côtes de Provence wines and local produce from the Maures. It's the natural starting point for a stroll toward the port and its roughly 800 boats. Your best bet: go before 10am, then have a coffee on promenade Aymeric Simon-Lorière.

⏱ 60 min

If you want to see Saint-Tropez without dealing with parking, board the Bateaux Verts from the port of Sainte-Maxime: the gulf crossing takes about twenty minutes. Sailings are frequent in season. Take the first morning departure; the 6pm return is packed.

⏱ 240 min

Parc Saint Donat

🛏️ Suggested base : Sainte Maxime · 9 km
★★★★☆
1

A phonograph museum in the heart of Provence is unexpected: the Musée du Phonographe et de la Musique mécanique is in parc Saint-Donat, between Sainte-Maxime and Le Muy, with more than 300 devices. Hours are limited and seasonal. Call before making the trip; it would be a shame to find it closed.

⏱ 60 min

Activities

If these machines appeal to you, ask for a demonstration at the Musée du Phonographe in parc Saint-Donat: some of the devices still work more than a century later. The museum is private and has no fixed hours. Calling ahead is not a formality; it's a condition of entry.

⏱ 60 min

Port Grimaud

🛏️ Suggested base : Grimaud · 5 km
★★★★☆
1

Kitsch to some, a masterpiece to others: Port Grimaud, designed from 1966 onward by Alsatian architect François Spoerry on marshland, holds the Architecture contemporaine remarquable label. Islands linked by bridges, more than seven kilometers of canals, each house moored to the water. The town is pedestrian-only: park at parking Nord or the La Foux parking lot.

⏱ 90 min
2

Its stained glass windows are by Victor Vasarely and depict the sun's course throughout the day: the Saint Francis of Assisi church, in the center of Port Grimaud, is ecumenical and deliberately restrained. Spoerry is buried there. You can climb the bell tower for €1, and ticket sales fund the church's upkeep. Allow fifteen to twenty minutes, including the view.

⏱ 20 min

Activities

Board a waterbus to see Port Grimaud from its canals: these shuttles were originally designed for residents before they began carrying visitors. Views unfold from one porch to the next, from the bell tower to the cast-iron bridges. Between 10am and 1pm, the views are clearest: after that, the light flattens everything.

⏱ 45 min

If you happen by on a Thursday or Sunday morning, place du Marché in Port Grimaud fills with fruit, vegetables, goat cheeses, olive oils and soaps. Producers pack up around 12:30pm. Come early, leave with lunch, and eat it on the beach rather than on a terrace.

⏱ 60 min

Grimaud

🛏️ Suggested base : Grimaud
★★★☆☆
1

Grimaud Castle overlooks the village from its rocky peak: a medieval ruin listed as a historic monument, with its castrum mentioned in texts as early as 1058. From up there, the whole Gulf of Saint-Tropez spreads out below and the Maures massif forms the horizon. Climb up at the end of the day; the low-angle light does all the work.

⏱ 60 min
2

Built between the late 12th and early 13th centuries, Grimaud's Saint-Michel church is listed as a historic monument and exemplifies unadorned Provençal Romanesque architecture. It was long the most imposing church in the area. The interior is dark and cool: a good stop when the village bakes at 3pm.

⏱ 30 min
3

A restored mill that no longer grinds: the Saint-Roch mill, on Grimaud's esplanade, was restored in the 1990s, but masonry damage during a test run put it permanently out of action. A windmill has been documented here since the 16th century under the name moulin de la Gardiole. The Fête du Moulin in June remains the best time to see the place come alive.

⏱ 30 min

Grimaud's wine estates offer more than postcard scenery: Côtes de Provence tastings a few minutes from the village, without the Saint-Tropez crowds. In moderation, of course, and with a designated driver. Call the day before: many welcome visitors only by appointment outside the tourist season.

Pont Des Fees

🛏️ Suggested base : Grimaud · 0 km
★★★★☆

A former aqueduct bridge, the Pont des Fées supplied Grimaud with water before becoming a walking destination. It marks the village's lowest point, tucked into a valley in the Maures massif. Be aware: routes suggested by apps sometimes lead to a dead end. Start from the cemetery parking lot; it's a few minutes away on foot.

⏱ 45 min

Activities

Start from the Saint-Roch mill to reach the Pont des Fées on foot: the trail winds through the scrubland, with views of Grimaud Castle reappearing on the way back. The route is marked and short. Avoid midday in July: there's nowhere to get water along the route, and the valley radiates heat.

⏱ 90 min

La Garde Freinet

🛏️ Suggested base : La Garde Freinet
★★★☆☆
1

A free museum dedicated to cork, silkworms and chestnuts: the Conservatoire du Patrimoine du Freinet, housed in the Saint-Jean chapel, tells the story of what sustained the Maures massif before tourism. A model of Fort Freinet and finds from excavations complete the visit. Open Monday to Friday: it's closed on weekends for most of the year.

⏱ 60 min

Activities

Head down into the lanes of La Garde-Freinet: the village took shape at the pass in the 14th century, when the inhabitants of Fort Freinet abandoned the rocky peak. Houses grew up around the Saint-Clément church, and fountains, a washhouse and a threshing floor line the route. A printed guide is available free at the tourist office.

⏱ 90 min

Chestnut honey and candied chestnuts are the signature of La Garde-Freinet, along with farmhouse goat cheeses and AOC olive oil. The village market is the place to taste all that at once. In autumn, it's chestnut season, and that changes everything.

⏱ 60 min

Fort Freinet

🛏️ Suggested base : La Garde Freinet · 1 km
★★★★☆
1

Fort Freinet occupies a rocky peak at 450 meters above La Garde-Freinet, protected by a ditch cut into the rock, 8 to 10 meters deep. The outlines of the 12th-century walls and main street can still be made out on the ground. The site was long wrongly attributed to the Saracens. Access is via a steep trail: about 45 minutes uphill, with suitable footwear.

⏱ 150 min

Activities

If you want to understand what you're looking at, book the guided tour of Fort Freinet through the Conservatoire du Patrimoine du Freinet: the guide recounts the history of the archaeological site and its abandonment. It's free for members and children under 8. Book online for a specific date: slots are scarce outside the tourist season.

⏱ 150 min

Lac Des Escarcets

🛏️ Suggested base : La Garde Freinet · 6 km
★★★★☆
1

An artificial lake dug for firefighting, now a bird refuge: Lake Escarcets, in the heart of the Plaine des Maures National Nature Reserve, belongs to the Conservatoire du littoral. Its reed bed provides a nesting area. A trail circles it, with information panels along the way. Access is via the piste de la Tire off the D558 toward La Garde-Freinet.

⏱ 60 min
2

At sunset, the pink sandstone slabs of the Plaine des Maures, dotted with umbrella pines and cork oaks, evoke a savanna. The reserve, created in 2009, covers 5,276 hectares. The August 2021 fires destroyed a large part: the landscape is rebuilding before your eyes. Stay on marked trails, the grasslands are very sensitive to trampling.

⏱ 60 min

Activities

If you're looking for Hermann's tortoise, it's here or in Corsica: the Plaine des Maures is its most important population stronghold in Provence and is covered by a national action plan. The European pond turtle and the ocellated lizard also live there. In the morning, tortoises warm up at the edges of bushes. Look, don't touch, don't collect anything.

⏱ 90 min

Bring binoculars on your walk around Lake Escarcets: harriers, teal, ducks and European bee-eaters visit the reed bed depending on the season. The walk is flat and short, suitable for families. Access to the Var's forested hills is restricted from June 21 to September 20 due to fire risk: check the prefecture's decree for the day.

⏱ 90 min

Where to stay in Lac Des Escarcets

🗺️ See hotels on the map
CarDrive to next stop: 4 km · 18min

Bois Du Rouquan

🛏️ Suggested base : Les Arcs Sur Argens · 12 km
★★★☆☆
1

The Rouquan woods, near Vidauban, contain a restored pitch kiln. Until the mid-19th century, pitch was produced here to seal the hulls and ropes of ships from Toulon and Saint-Tropez. The loop is an easy 4.1 km. It starts 8 km from the village, on the D48 toward La Garde-Freinet.

⏱ 120 min

Activities

Walk the Rouquan woods loop, staying on the tracks throughout: the area is part of the Plaine des Maures Nature Reserve, a refuge for Hermann's tortoise. Start at the rest area, near the second water tank on the right. Let's be frank: you come for the kiln, not the panorama.

The Sainte-Brigitte chapel crowns a 184-meter conical hill above Vidauban. Dating from the 17th century, it commemorates Bridget of Sweden's supposed passage through Provence. Struck by lightning in the 1970s, it had its roof restored in 1998. A winding path climbs to it from a free parking lot: allow just under an hour for the round trip from the center.

⏱ 60 min

Activities

Canoe down the Argens from Vidauban: the river winds through an alluvial plain between riverside woodland and vineyards. Its tributary, the Aille, has waterfalls and a long rocky plateau nearby. In summer, the flow can be low: call the rental operator before making the trip.

Les Arcs Sur Argens

🛏️ Suggested base : Les Arcs Sur Argens
★★★☆☆
1

Locals call it the Tour Sarrasine; it's actually the keep of the Villeneuve family, Catalan lords who settled in Les Arcs-sur-Argens from the 13th century onward. Standing 19 meters tall, it dominates the village and survived the castle's destruction, ordered by Barras during the Revolution, thanks to his secretary, a native of the village. Climb up along the cobbled lanes: they're steep and paved.

⏱ 45 min
2

Le Parage is the medieval quarter of Les Arcs-sur-Argens: its name comes from the Occitan paratge, meaning nobility. Four gates punctuate the defensive walls, including the Porte du Miracle des Roses. The clock tower, formerly a 14th-century flanking tower, is topped by a bell frame dating from 1662. The quarter was saved from ruin in the 1960s by a handful of enthusiasts.

⏱ 75 min
3

It houses a Louis Bréa altarpiece dated 1501: the Saint-Jean-Baptiste church in Les Arcs-sur-Argens replaced the old Parage church in the 19th century. There's also an animated Provençal nativity scene. Visit it on your way down from the upper quarter, so save it for the end of the route.

⏱ 30 min

Activities

Step inside the Maison des Vins Côtes de Provence in Les Arcs-sur-Argens: several hundred wines gathered in one place, to help you understand the appellation without visiting estate after estate. Taste in moderation, with a designated driver. Rosé is the obvious choice, but ask for the reds: that's where the surprises lie.

⏱ 90 min

If you're traveling with children, the Réal Max Carzoli walk, in Les Arcs-sur-Argens, is less than a kilometer between the stream and the countryside. It's a shaded green corridor, accessible from the center. Perfect for a quiet hour waiting for the afternoon opening of Sainte-Roseline chapel.

⏱ 45 min

A mummy and a Chagall in the same room: the Sainte-Roseline chapel, built in the 11th century and listed in 1980, displays the remains of Roseline de Villeneuve in a crystal reliquary, opposite the mosaic Le Repas des Anges, donated by Marc Chagall and unveiled in 1975. Stained glass by Bazaine and Ubac, bronzes by Diego Giacometti. Open only in the afternoon, closed Mondays.

2

Restored in 1969 thanks to Marguerite Maeght's patronage, the Sainte-Roseline chapel adjoins the cloister of the former monastery of La Celle-Roubaud. Marguerite Maeght had to go to court to have the site opened to the public. You can visit the cloister when access is available: ask on site, as it isn't always open.

⏱ 30 min

Activities

Walk down the avenue of plane trees to Château Sainte-Roseline, a Côtes de Provence cru classé right next to the chapel. Tastings and sales amid the vineyards surrounding the site. There's a large parking lot almost opposite: it's the simplest way to visit both without getting back on the road.

Le Muy

🛏️ Suggested base : Bagnols En Foret · 13 km
★★☆☆☆
1

Documented as early as 1252, the Tour Charles Quint in Le Muy was called Tour Notre-Dame before 1536. That year, residents barricaded themselves inside to try to assassinate the emperor invading Provence. They fatally wounded a well-dressed man they mistook for him: it was the poet Garcilaso de la Vega. They surrendered on a promise that their lives would be spared, and were hanged anyway.

⏱ 30 min
2

An 18th-century oil mill filled with gliders and jeeps: the Musée de la Libération du Muy, next to the Tour Charles Quint, tells the story of the airborne operation of August 15, 1944. Le Muy was one of the first towns liberated in Provence. Free entry, run by volunteers, but open only a few half-days: check the opening hours before you come.

⏱ 60 min

Activities

If you're there on a Thursday or Sunday, Le Muy's market coincides with the opening of the Tour Charles Quint and the Musée de la Libération. Visit all three in one go, between 9:30am and 12:30pm. The rest of the week, the village is very quiet and the doors are closed.

⏱ 60 min

Gorges De Pennafort

🛏️ Suggested base : Bagnols En Foret · 11 km
★★★★☆
1

The water is cold, the rock is red and the bottom of the Pennafort gorges stays cool when the coast swelters. The Rioufreid tumbles from pool to pool for about 400 meters, down to the waterfall. Be aware: a 1996 decree prohibits swimming, despite what most visitors do, and you can be fined.

⏱ 90 min
2

Built in 1855 on the remains of an 11th-century tower, the Notre-Dame de Pennafort chapel crowns a rocky spur where two valleys meet, in a Greek Revival style unusual for the region. A footpath leads up from the picnic area. Unobstructed views over the gorges, and usually nobody around.

⏱ 45 min

Activities

Follow the Rioufreid riverbed from the Pennafort gorges parking lot, on the D25 between Callas and Le Muy: 2.6 km round trip, some rocks to cross, feet sometimes in the water. Parking is free and quite large. Come in spring: in summer, the river dries up and there's not much left to see.

La Bouverie

🛏️ Suggested base : Bagnols En Foret · 6 km
★★☆☆☆
1

The Maison de la Préhistoire in La Bouverie is devoted to Bouverian man, the Upper Paleolithic human who gave his name to the region's last Paleolithic industry. Points, scrapers and knapped flint come from excavations led in 1967 by Jean Landréat and François Puigdellivol. Free entry, open only for half-day periods: call ahead.

⏱ 45 min
2

Four caves discovered in the 1970s at the foot of the Blavet gorges: the La Bouverie caves were occupied almost continuously during the last 20,000 years of the Upper Paleolithic. South-facing, with a stream nearby and shelter from the wind. You can see them from the trails, rather than on guided tours.

⏱ 45 min

Activities

If you're passing through on a Saturday morning, La Bouverie's market offers local produce in the northern district of Roquebrune-sur-Argens. Wine estates and an apiary round out the stop after your hike. It's the best place to stock up before tackling the Blavet gorges.

⏱ 60 min

Gorges Du Blavet

🛏️ Suggested base : Bagnols En Foret · 4 km
★★★★☆
1

Colorado in Provence: the Blavet gorges owe their red color to amaranth-red rhyolite, a volcanic rock from the Estérel massif. The Blavet, a tributary of the Argens, has carved a canyon of cliffs and rock spires here. The contrast with the cork oaks is stark. Low-angle morning or evening light brings out everything the rock has to offer.

⏱ 90 min
2

Rhyolite was extracted here until the 18th century to carve millstones for flour and oil mills. Remains of millstones survive along the Blavet gorges trail. The wild scenery is therefore partly a former industrial site. Spotting them requires attention: they're not signposted on the ground.

⏱ 30 min

Activities

Park at the Blavet gorges parking lot on the D47, on the Bagnols-en-Forêt side, for the orange-marked loop. Two fords, a steep, stony descent and a viewpoint orientation panel as your reward. Avoid this route in rainy weather: the rocks become as slippery as bars of soap and water levels at the fords rise quickly.

⏱ 180 min

If you're a climber, climbing is the best reason to come to the Blavet gorges: the rhyolite has a texture very different from the Var's limestone, and the site attracts climbing teams from far beyond the region. A climbing guide is sold at the Bagnols-en-Forêt tourist information office. There is a small but real risk of falling rocks below the cliff faces.

⏱ 240 min

Grotte Du Mueron

🛏️ Suggested base : Bagnols En Foret · 5 km
★★★★☆
1

The cave mouth suddenly comes into view at the foot of the cliff: Mueron Cave has a monumental entrance and extends far into the rhyolite. It was occupied in 10,000 BC, then served as a Bronze Age campsite. South-facing, with a commanding view over the valley and a stream below: it had everything. It still shelters hikers caught in thunderstorms.

⏱ 30 min
2

Two natural arches are tucked against the cliff face, about ten meters above the trail, a few steps from Mueron Cave. They go unnoticed unless you look for them. The cave itself is not very deep despite its monumental entrance. Look up just after the cave, or you'll walk past without seeing them.

⏱ 20 min

Activities

Approach along the orange-marked trail: there are two fords to cross before reaching Mueron Cave. The overhanging routes beneath the cave mouth make it one of the Var's major climbing spots. Good footwear is essential: the descent just beyond is steep and rutted by erosion.

⏱ 90 min

If you're not a climber, continue to the viewpoint orientation panel above Mueron Cave: the panorama takes in the Estérel, Roquebrune Rock and the Fréjus-Saint-Raphaël coast. Return along the Bayonne track, lined with chestnut trees.

The oldest church in Bagnols-en-Forêt is not in the village: the 11th-century Romanesque Saint-Denis chapel stands apart, at the end of a one-kilometer trail through vineyards. Built between 1704 and 1707 at the top of the village, Bagnols-en-Forêt's Saint-Antonin church is surprisingly bright: 30 meters long, 10 wide, tall, broad windows and two Louis XIII-style altarpieces. Its style combines Romanesque and Renaissance elements. The church square, shaded by horse chestnut trees, is the best place in the village to catch your breath.

⏱ 30 min
2

The former millstone quarries of Bagnols-en-Forêt are reached along the ridges amid red rocks. Stone was cut there from prehistory until the 18th century. In clear weather, the view stretches to the sea. Start from the village, but access to the hills is restricted in summer: check the day's decree before setting out.

Activities

Follow the Chemin de notre mémoire through the lanes of Bagnols-en-Forêt: old photos displayed on façades compare the village then and now. The route passes along rue en Calade, the main medieval approach from Fréjus, and past the Siagnole fountain. Free, one hour, best done first thing in the morning before the heat.

Lac De Saint Cassien

🛏️ Suggested base : Bagnols En Foret · 11 km
★★★★☆
1

A lake born of a catastrophe: EDF began the Saint-Cassien dam project after the Malpasset dam failed in 1959, and completed it in 1966. The reservoir holds about 60 million m³ across more than 400 hectares, between the Var and Alpes-Maritimes. The Maison du Lac, on the Tanneron side, serves as a gateway with its exhibition area about the Pays de Fayence.

⏱ 60 min

Activities

Rent a pedal boat or paddleboard on Lake Saint-Cassien: combustion engines are prohibited, leaving the water surprisingly calm for a lake this size. Several water sports centers share the shores, with a sailing school and mountain bike rentals. The free summer shuttle saves you the parking headache at the Maison du Lac.

⏱ 120 min

If you're traveling with young children, head for the beach below the Maison du Lac on Lake Saint-Cassien: swimming supervised by Var firefighters in summer, a first-aid station, and beach volleyball and pétanque nearby. Supervision runs from July 1 to August 31, from 11am to 7pm. Outside those dates and hours, nobody is on duty.

Agay

🛏️ Suggested base : Saint Raphael · 7 km
★★★★☆
1

Agay means favorable in Greek, and sailors have never disputed that: the bay, tucked between Cap Dramont and Pointe de la Baumette, is one of the best sheltered on the coast. Three sandy beaches, the Rastel d'Agay and its red rocks in the background, and a small marina. In season, parking spaces fill up before 10am.

⏱ 60 min
2

The arrival of the railway in 1860 made Agay a stopover for artists: Maupassant, Louis Valtat, Vincent d'Indy, Saint-Exupéry. A fountain dedicated to the Little Prince pays tribute to him in the hamlet. At the foot of the Baumette lighthouse, a stele marks the spot where his plane was last spotted, on July 31, 1944.

⏱ 45 min

Activities

Paddle from Agay beach toward the Estérel coves: kayaks and paddleboards are available to rent on site, the water is clear and the red rock drops straight into the sea. The beach slopes gently and has Handiplage and AudioPlage certification, with a lifting hoist and wheelchairs for entering the water. Dogs are prohibited from June 15 to September 15.

Cap Dramont

🛏️ Suggested base : Saint Raphael · 6 km
★★★★☆
1

The only blue pebble beach around: Débarquement beach, at the foot of Cap Dramont, owes its stones to esterellite, while all the surrounding landscape is red. On August 15, 1944, more than 20,000 GIs from the Texas 36th Division landed there. A commemorative stele marks the place. Supervised swimming in season, and good waves for surfing.

⏱ 60 min
2

Built in 1860 on the ruins of a 1562 watchtower, the coastal lookout station at Cap Dramont still monitors the sea, including for pollution control. The building itself is closed to the public. The viewpoint just behind it, however, overlooks the bay of Saint-Raphaël, the Île d'Or and the Estérel massif. That's why you make the climb.

⏱ 60 min

Activities

Walk around Cap Dramont along the coastal path, from Camp Long to the Poussaï fishing port: about 3.5 km from Débarquement beach, with QR codes on the rocks explaining the wildlife, plants and geology. The beach parking lot is undergoing work and may start charging: bring change.

The Île d'Or is mainly worthwhile for its history: a doctor, Auguste Lutaud, supposedly won it at cards at the beginning of the 20th century, proclaimed himself Auguste I and had a square tower built there in red stone from the Estérel. Many think Hergé drew inspiration from it for The Black Island. It has remained private property since 1897: content yourself with the view.

Activities

Rent a kayak at Débarquement beach and paddle around the Île d'Or: the water is clear, the rocky seabed is worth bringing a mask for, and the red tower comes into view from every angle. Landing is prohibited; the islet is private. Calm seas are essential: choppy waves build quickly in the passage.

Saint Raphael

🛏️ Suggested base : Saint Raphael
★★★★☆
1

The Notre-Dame de la Victoire basilica rises with its neo-Byzantine domes in the heart of Saint-Raphaël: built between 1882 and 1889 by Pierre Aublé in pink Estérel sandstone, it covers 850 m² and stands 35 meters high. Its name recalls the naval battle of October 7, 1571. The Vatican granted it basilica status in 2004. Walk around the outside before entering: that's where the details are.

⏱ 45 min
2

129 steps, and the best viewpoint in Saint-Raphaël: the 22-meter tower of the Romanesque San Rafeu church offers a panorama from the Estérel to the Villepey ponds and as far as Roquebrune Rock. The church dates from the 12th century and is listed as a historic monument. Climb early in the day: the light is better and the staircase less stifling.

⏱ 45 min
3

Housed in the former 12th-century rectory, Saint-Raphaël's archaeological museum displays amphoras and artifacts from underwater excavations, as well as bas-reliefs from the former Carolingian church. Ramparts and arrow slits can still be made out in the walls. It's the perfect plan B on a rainy day or when the mistral blows.

⏱ 60 min

Activities

Walk through the flower and vegetable market in Saint-Raphaël's old town: it's held daily in the narrow, shaded lanes of the old village quarter. It's what remains of agricultural Saint-Raphaël, before the casino and villas. Continue to the old port, three minutes away, for a coffee overlooking the boats.

⏱ 60 min

If you prefer walking to sightseeing, Saint-Raphaël's street art route links works by artists using very different techniques across the city. Free, outdoors and accessible at any time. Pick up the map at the tourist office on quai Albert 1er.

Frejus

🛏️ Suggested base : Frejus
★★★★☆
1

Fréjus' amphitheater divides opinion, and it's easy to see why: the restoration begun in 2007 extended the ancient ruins with modern materials rather than reconstructing them. Built in the 1st century and measuring 113 meters by 85, it could accommodate up to 12,000 spectators. Victor Hugo saw horses grazing there in 1839. If the concrete makes you bristle, seeing the outside is more than enough.

⏱ 45 min
2

Fréjus is nicknamed the Provençal Pompeii, and place Formigé explains why: Saint-Léonce cathedral, the cloister, baptistery and episcopal palace form a single episcopal complex. The octagonal 5th-century baptistery is one of the oldest in France and is still used for baptisms. A guided tour is included in the ticket: take it, as it's the only way to enter the baptistery.

⏱ 75 min
3

A fantastical bestiary looks down at you from the ceiling: the larch ceiling coffers in the cloister of Saint-Léonce cathedral in Fréjus are covered with figures painted in the 14th century, human, animal or somewhere in between. They've darkened over time, but many can still be made out. An indoor room shows an explanatory video: watch it before, not after.

⏱ 45 min
4

If the arena left you cold, the Fréjus aqueduct makes up for it: it brought water from the Siagnole, in Mons, over about forty kilometers. Its remains are distributed between avenue des Aqueducs, rue Henri Vadon and the Villa Aurélienne park, which preserves the largest portion. The park is free and shaded.

⏱ 45 min

Activities

Get the Fréjus Pass if you plan to visit several sites: €6 for four sites, valid for seven days, versus €3 for the amphitheater alone. It covers the ancient and medieval heritage of the city, which holds the Ville et Pays d'art et d'histoire label. The pass pays for itself from the second site: easy enough in Fréjus.

⏱ 30 min

If you prefer the unusual to the Roman, head to the north of Fréjus: the Missiri mosque rises among holm oaks and stone pines, and the Hong Hien pagoda completes the picture. Two colonial legacies you would not expect here, ten minutes from the arena. The mosque cannot be visited and is seen from the outside only; for the pagoda, check the opening hours, they are irregular.

⏱ 90 min

Etangs De Villepey

🛏️ Suggested base : Frejus · 4 km
★★★★☆
1

Locals call it little Camargue: the Villepey ponds, in the Argens delta, form one of the few coastal wetlands between the Camargue and the Italian border. About 260 hectares, owned by the Conservatoire du littoral following acquisitions in 1982 and 1997, and designated under the Ramsar Convention in 2008. Flamingos, herons and egrets depending on the season.

⏱ 60 min
2

More than 220 bird species have been recorded at the Villepey ponds, including notable breeding species such as the little bittern. The European pond turtle also hides here, keeping a lower profile. The Vasière bird hide lets you watch without disturbing the wildlife. March and early September, during migration: that's when it's worth the trip.

⏱ 60 min

Activities

Park at the Esclamandes beach parking lot and follow the Villepey ponds trail: 7.8 km, 14 meters of elevation gain, two hours and fifteen minutes. Wooden walkways, reed beds and a dune belt. Some bridges remain inaccessible after flooding, and one section closes from June 15 to September 15: plan an out-and-back walk rather than a loop.

⏱ 135 min

Sea daffodils grow in the sand of the dune belt at the Villepey ponds, alongside sea holly and prickly parsnip. A one-kilometer loop on the Esclamandes side is enough to see them. These plants are protected: look, don't pick them, and stay on the marked trail.

⏱ 45 min
